# SK4024 — `GC.Collect` is called from application code

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A forced collection suspends every thread and promotes what survives, so it usually makes the pressure it was added to relieve permanent.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Performance |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.3 |
| Supersedes | S1215 |

## Why

`GC.Collect` is almost always added after a memory graph looked wrong, and it is the one response that cannot help. The collector's generational assumption is that most objects die young; a collection forced at an arbitrary moment finds the young objects still live, promotes them to a longer-lived generation, and thereby guarantees that the next collection to reach them is a more expensive one. Meanwhile every managed thread is suspended for the duration. The cost is paid at every call and the benefit is a number in a profiler that looks better for one sample. What the call is standing in for is an allocation that should not happen, a buffer that should be pooled, or a handle that should be disposed — and none of those is an edit an analyzer can write, which is why this rule reports and does not fix.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
void Refresh() {
    cache.Clear();
    GC.Collect();
}
```

Write:

```csharp
void Refresh() {
    cache.Clear();
}
```

## When it does not fire

Every overload of `System.GC.Collect` is reported, resolved through the semantic model rather than matched on the written name. ⚠ **There is no fix**, and the rule says so in `rules.json` rather than offering the deletion: the call is a symptom, and removing it without dealing with what it was compensating for changes the program's memory behaviour in a direction nobody measured. ⚠ **Measurement code is the one legitimate caller and is excluded**: a method or type carrying a test or benchmark attribute — `Fact`, `Theory`, `Test`, `TestCase`, `TestMethod`, `Benchmark` and the BenchmarkDotNet setup and cleanup markers — establishes a known heap on purpose, and reporting there would be reporting the measurement rather than the program. A finaliser-behaviour test outside those attributes, and a deliberate collection at a genuine idle point in a desktop application, are real callers the rule still reports; they are the case for a suppression with a reason, which is what `SK7071` and the baseline are for.
